extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claims for patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the MPEP flowchart and the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 1, 2A, 2B) including Pathways A–C, claim construction (BRI), and treatment of judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the eligibility flowchart and three pathways (A, B, C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim satisfies subject matter eligibility criteria by evaluating the claim in accordance with the MPEP flowchart which illustrates steps for products and processes during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The flowchart shows Step 1 (statutory categories), Step 2 (Alice/Mayo two-part test, implemented as Steps 2A and 2B), and three eligibility pathways: Pathway A (streamlined/self-evident eligibility), Pathway B (Step 1 YES and not directed to a judicial exception — Step 2A NO), and Pathway C (Step 1 YES, Step 2A YES, but additional elements amount to significantly more — Step 2B YES). If a claim is not eligible under any pathway, it is patent ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If uncertain about streamlined analysis, conduct full analysis. Regardless of 101 outcome, examine other requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, utility, inventorship, double patenting). See MPEP §§ 2106.04–2106.06 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Claim must fall within one of the four statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (the four statutory categories of invention under 35 U.S.C. 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any category (Step 1: NO), it is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). It is not necessary to identify a single correct category so long as the claim clearly falls within at least one. If the BRI of the claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1 and should be rejected; best practice is to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a process (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'process' defines actions and is claimed as an act or step, or a series of acts or steps; synonymous with 'method' (35 U.S.C. 100(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Gottschalk v. Benson and related cases: process requires action (e.g., a mode of treatment performed upon subject-matter to transform it). Evaluate whether claimed steps amount to a process rather than an abstract recitation. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a machine (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'machine' is a concrete thing consisting of parts or devices; includes mechanical devices or combinations of mechanical powers and devices to perform functions and produce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, verify the invention is a concrete thing with parts/devices. Examples and caselaw (Digitech, Burr) cited. A machine generally exists in physical/tangible form. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a manufacture (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'manufacture' is a tangible article given a new form, quality, property, or combination through man-made or artificial means (products of manufacturing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufactures include products made by giving new forms/properties to raw materials and can include parts of machines considered separately. Use court definitions (Digitech, Diamond, Samsung). Verify tangible article resulted from manufacturing process. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a composition of matter (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'composition of matter' is a combination of two or more substances and includes composite articles (chemical unions or mechanical mixtures, gases, fluids, powders, solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed invention is a combination of substances or composite article (e.g., genetically modified microorganism treated as composition/manufacture). Cite Digitech, Chakrabarty. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory product examples (Step 1 guidance on intangible products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Products that do not have a physical or tangible form do not fall within the machine/manufacture/composition categories (e.g., information/data per se, computer program per se, transitory signals per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to software 'detached from any medium' or an intangible collection of information lacks physical/tangible form and is non-statutory (e.g., Digitech, Microsoft v. AT&T, Benson). Transitory propagating signals are physical but lack concrete structure and are non-statutory (Nuijten, Mentor Graphics). If BRI encompasses such non-statutory embodiments (e.g., computer-readable medium that can be a carrier wave), rejection is appropriate. See MPEP § 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 1 and later steps after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims according to their BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If BRI of the claim covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, claim fails Step 1. Examiners should point out BRI and recommend narrowing amendments when appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 and § 2106 subsections II–III for BRI importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A overall: Determine if claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A (first part of Alice/Mayo test) asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea; if so, further analysis at Step 2B is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Step 2A after claim construction/BRI. If claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B. If it is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B to determine if additional elements amount to 'significantly more.' See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether the claim 'recites' (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon — i.e., whether a judicial exception is explicitly stated or described in the claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'recites' (sets forth/ describes) from merely 'involves' — claims that merely involve an exception may still be eligible. Examples: Diehr/Mayo claims that 'set forth' exceptions vs Alice claims that 'describe' the concept. If Prong One is met, evaluate Prong Two; if not, claim is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO). See MPEP § 2106.04(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two: Does the claim integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether additional claim elements integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application; if so, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application of the exception, then claim avoids being 'directed to' the exception. Mere recitation of an exception or adding only another judicial exception is insufficient to integrate. See MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2) and Alice Corp. guidance. If Prong Two fails, proceed to Step 2B to assess whether elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions defined and preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions include 'laws of nature,' 'natural phenomena,' and 'abstract ideas' (described variously as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, mathematical algorithms/formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The underlying concern is preemption — patents should not monopolize basic tools of scientific and technological work. However, preemption is not a standalone test; the Alice/Mayo two-part framework resolves preemption concerns. Courts have held that newly discovered exceptions are still exceptions (Myriad, Mayo, Flook). Absence of complete preemption does not automatically mean eligibility. See MPEP § 2106.04 and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple judicial exceptions: how to analyze
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may recite multiple judicial exceptions; examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions and should avoid unnecessarily parsing claims into multiple exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, treat multiple abstract ideas together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. If exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), examiners may select one exception and conduct the analysis on that selected exception for examination efficiency — if selected-exception analysis shows integration or significantly more, claim should be considered eligible. If not, and no other elements amount to significantly more, the claim is ineligible. See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of mere additional judicial-exception elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim contains no additional elements beyond the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application or to show significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding one abstract idea to another does not render the claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). For eligibility, additional elements must transform the claim into a patent-eligible application (Alice Corp.). If no sufficient additional elements, make appropriate rejection and recommend amendment if possible. See MPEP § 2106.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner best practices when claim fails Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim fails Step 1 or is directed to a judicial exception without integration, examiners should make the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and recommend claim amendments where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim fails Step 1 (non-statutory), use form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 and recommend an amendment to resolve eligibility. If claim recites an exception and has insufficient additional elements, indicate deficiency and recommend amendments. If uncertain about streamlined Pathway A, perform full analysis to ensure consistency. See MPEP §§ 2106.03–2106.07.
